Higher or lower would both count, so surprise lives in both tails. A five percent test puts two and a half percent in each, beyond one point nine six. A one-sided test spends all five percent in one tail, so its cutoff is nearer, at one point six four five. That's an easier bar to clear... which is exactly why the side has to be chosen before you see the data. So what is that three percent, exactly?

Take a simpler case. A friend's coin lands heads sixty-two times in a hundred flips. Assume it's fair, and simulate a hundred flips, a hundred thousand times over. That pile is the null distribution. Sixty-two sits twelve from the middle. So does thirty-eight. Now count every run at least that far out. Two point one percent of them. That's all a p-value is: the share of the null world at least as extreme as what you saw. An area, not a verdict. And that tells you what it can't be.

A p-value is NOT the chance the null is true. It was computed by assuming the null. The chance of the data, given the null, isn't the chance of the null, given the data. Swap them, and you've made the prosecutor's fallacy. Nor is it the size of an effect. Hold a tiny effect fixed, and only grow the sample. Twenty per group, p is point eight three. A thousand, point zero zero zero four. A hundred thousand, and it prints as zero. The effect never changed. Only how much data could see it. Which leads to the easiest way to fool yourself.

When the null is true, a p-value is just a random number. Every value from zero to one is equally likely. So run twenty tests where nothing is real, and you should expect one under point zero five. Here, it's test fourteen, at point zero three three. Report only that one, and you've turned luck into a discovery. That's p-hacking.
